newsitem.title: PERU: Peru media questions legitimacy of Fujimori's rule.
newsitem.headline: Peru media questions legitimacy of Fujimori's rule.

text.p: Sections of the media opposed to President Alberto Fujimori questioned on Thursday his right to rule because of doubts obout his birthplace. The constitution says the president must be born in Peru.

The weelky magazine Caretas published an investigation examining the authenticity of documents stating Fujimori -- the 58-year-old son of Japanese immigrants -- was born in Peru and questioning if in fact he was born in Japan.
Government Palace spokesman Ysrael Mertz told Reuters he had no official comment on the Caretas report, which the opposition daily La Republica and Uranio 15 television station also publicised.

Government congressmen said the report was part of an opposition campaign to stain the president's image. Some legislators also said they feared that questionining Fujimori's legitimacy to rule heightened the chances of a military coup.

"Those responsible for releasing this news know perfectly well that even the smallest suspicion about President Fujimori's nationality could cause rifts and possibly lead to a coup in Peru," independent congressmen Jose Barba told local radio station Radioprogramas.

The Caretas report, based on a four-year investigation, showed allegedly falsified documents, which apparently altered information on Fujimori's birthdate and suggested he may have entered Peru from Japan only after he was born.

But local government spokesmen from the municipality of Fujimori's official birthplace -- Miraflores in Lima -- said there were no irregularities in the documents stating where the president was born.

Fujimori's popularity has plummeted in recent weeks to its lowest point since he took office in 1990 and a series of scandals involving alleged abuses of power by the security forces have sparked violent street protests.

Most Peruvians criticise Fujimori for his authoritarian style. But they also believe the head of Peru's intelligence service, Vladimiro Montesinos, and the country's armed forces chief Gen. Nicolas Bari de Hermoza wield more power than the president, according to local pollsters.

The former head of Fujimori's election campaign, Francisco Loayza, claimed Montesinos knew the president was born in Japan and used the information to blackmail him into granting increased powers to the security forces.
